#

# failing, is the mechanism the framework ships. Using it on ourselves is the only way to find out

# and "this rule is inconvenient" a thing the repository has actually had to answer for.

# as-a-pass invariant, and the explainability of what we emit.

cases.input:
# Mathematics standards policy for this project.
#
# This file declares what applies here. It is the only place a project may say a rule does not apply,
# is knowingly unmet, or has been satisfied by human review — and the three are different mechanisms
# that must not be confused for one another:
#
#   applicability: not-applicable   the rule has no subject in this project
#   exceptions:                     the rule applies and the project knowingly does not satisfy it
#   attestations:                   the rule applies and a human established that it is satisfied
#
# A fourth outcome needs no declaration and is the most common: the rule applies, nothing evaluated
# it, and the report says `not-evaluated` rather than pretending it passed.

standardVersion: "1.0.0"
project: "<your project name>"

mathematics:
  # Which of the five regimes describe this project (Standard 1 R1). A claim about the PROJECT, not
  # about the standards — it stops being true the moment you acquire the capability you disclaimed.
  regimes:
    - informal
    # - computational
    # - formal
    # - theorem-proving
    # - open-problem

  # Where the claims ledger lives. Default shown; change it only if you have a reason.
  claimsLedger: "artifacts/claims-ledger.md"

  # Uncomment when you use a proof assistant. Scanning covers all three regardless; declaring them
  # records what a reader of a formal claim is being asked to trust.
  # proofAssistants:
  #   - lean4

  # Set true when working toward a major open problem. This turns on Standard 17's higher bar: the
  # per-problem tracking record becomes required, and so do stopping criteria.
  # openProblemMode: true
  # openProblemsDir: "artifacts/open-problems"

# --- Applicability -------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# Every not-applicable declaration needs a reason AND a revisitWhen naming the event that would end
# it. `math-standards policy` rejects one without a revisit condition, because a classification with
# no end condition is a permanent exemption wearing a temporary label.
#
# Example — a project with no proof assistant:
#
# applicability:
#   formal.trusted-chain-tracked:
#     status: not-applicable
#     reason: "This project contains no proof-assistant sources."
#     reviewedAt: "2026-01-01"
#     revisitWhen: "A .lean, .v, or .thy file is added to this repository."

# --- Exceptions ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# A time-bounded, approved waiver of a rule that DOES apply. An expired exception is a compliance
# failure, not a resolution.
#
# An exception against a rule the catalog marks `forbidden` and `nonExemptible` is REJECTED, and the
# rejection is itself a failure. That is what makes a prohibition a prohibition: a rule a policy
# could waive would not be one.
#
# exceptions:
#   - rule: computation.scope-declared
#     reason: "The 2024 scans predate this standard; they are being re-run with full metadata."
#     approvedBy: "<name>"
#     approvedAt: "2026-01-01"
#     expires: "2026-06-01"
#     reference: "artifacts/adr/0003-rescanning-legacy-computations.md"

# --- Attestations --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# Most of what these standards require is mathematical judgement, so this is where most of the real
# assurance lives. An attestation is evidence, not a waiver:
#
#   * it never overrides an automated finding — a contradicted attestation fails;
#   * it goes stale, back to not-evaluated, when the files it reviewed change;
#   * it can record a REJECTION, which is a first-class outcome. A system that only lets a human
#     record approval has decided in advance what the human will say.
#
# Omit `digest` on the first pass: `math-standards validate` prints the current digest so you can
# record it.
#
# attestations:
#   rigor.unjustified-division:
#     status: approved
#     reviewedBy: "<name>"
#     reviewedAt: "2026-01-15"
#     evidence: "Checked every cancellation in proofs/clm-0002.md; each denominator is non-vanishing on the stated domain by Lemma CLM-0005."
#     reviewedAgainst:
#       paths:
#         - "proofs/clm-0002.md"

# The AFTER half of the escape-hatch pair: the same repository, plus one line that is not true.
#
# Byte-identical to `escape-hatch-undeclared` apart from the `artifacts.failedRoutes` block below,
# which names a file that does not exist. Step 4 made this rule stop failing and start reporting
# `skipped / not-evaluated` — correctly, because the framework could not read the evidence and being
# unable to look is not an observation about what would have been seen.
#
# But `skipped` leaves the score's denominator and the failure list, so at step 4 this fixture scored
# HIGHER than its honest twin and was one rule away from COMPLIANT. A better verdict, bought by
# naming a file that is not there. That is §0m one level up, and step 5 closes it:
#
#     score(with an unresolved required pointer) <= score(without the pointer)
#
# and the terminal status may never improve either. The mechanism is not to restore the failure —
# the framework still does not know whether this project preserves its failed routes — but to give
# the unresolved rule a zero-credit place in the denominator and to let an aggregate
# `unresolvedRequired` condition carry the verdict.
standardVersion: "1.0.0"
project: "escape-hatch-declared"

artifacts:
  failedRoutes: "docs/ABANDONED_ROUTES.md"

mathematics:
  regimes:
    - open-problem
  openProblemMode: true

cases.name: 0288fce:test/fixtures/stale-attestation/project-policy.yml
cases.input:
# An attestation that HAS a digest, and whose digest no longer matches what is there.
#
# The reviewer looked, wrote down what they looked at, and recorded the digest of it — the whole
# mechanism working as designed. Then the file changed. The engine is right to stop honouring the
# attestation: what was reviewed is not what is there now.
#
# What it does with it is the defect this fixture pins. A stale attestation returns the rule to
# not-evaluated, and at 6eadfe0 that is indistinguishable in the output from a rule nobody ever
# attested. Three different situations —
#
#     nobody reviewed this            (never attested)
#     nothing was there to inspect    (no-subject)
#     somebody reviewed something else (stale)
#
# — arrive at the same `skipped / not-evaluated` with the same message, and only the last one names
# a person who did work that has since expired. A reader who cannot tell them apart cannot tell
# which one they are supposed to act on.
standardVersion: "1.0.0"
project: "stale-attestation"

mathematics:
  regimes:
    - informal
  claimsLedger: "artifacts/claims-ledger.md"

attestations:
  evidence.discarded-failures:
    status: approved
    reviewedBy: "A. Reviewer"
    reviewedAt: "2026-06-01"
    evidence: "Read notes/abandoned.md in full. Every route tried is recorded with the reason it was dropped."
    reviewedAgainst:
      paths:
        - "notes/abandoned.md"
      digest: "00000000000000000000000000000000"

# An adopter with no provenance evidence of its own.
#
# At 03f44d6 `integrity.provenance-digest` passes here, and what it certifies is that
# MathematicsStandards' source documents are unmodified — a true statement about the framework,
# counted inside this project's compliance score. Every adopter gets the same row for the same
# reason, and none of them can affect it.
#
# The claim: the result stays (the framework auditing itself during an adopter's run is useful, and
# §0h says so explicitly), it says `subject: framework`, and it leaves the adopter's score. A number
# describing this project must be computed only from rules about this project.
#
# See wrong-root-broken/project-policy.yml for the other half of the pair.

project: "wrong-root-absent"

mathematics:
  regimes:
    - informal

cases.name: 0288fce:test/fixtures/wrong-root-broken/project-policy.yml
cases.input:
# An adopter carrying a drifted provenance record of its own.
#
# artifacts/provenance-digests.json here records a digest that does not match the file it names. That
# is the exact condition `integrity.provenance-digest` exists to catch — and this fixture asserts
# that the rule must NOT catch it, which is the opposite of the obvious reading and is the point.
#
# `integrity.provenance-digest` is a rule about the standards pack: its own catalog text is "the
# SHA-256 of each file listed in artifacts/provenance-digests.json … matches the recorded digest",
# meaning MathematicsStandards' source documents. An adopter does not own those documents and has no
# rule catalog, so the §0h repair is not "read the adopter's root instead" — that would export the
# framework's housekeeping as an adopter obligation. It is that the result must say whose property it
# is about, and must not enter a score that purports to describe the adopter.
#
# Hence the pair, which together prove the subject separated rather than merely relocated:
#
#   this fixture        adopter's own record is drifted  → framework-subject result UNCHANGED
#                                                          (an adopter cannot make the framework
#                                                          fail its own integrity check)
#   wrong-root-absent   adopter has no record at all     → result unchanged, and OUT of their score
#                                                          (the framework's clean record cannot
#                                                          flatter the adopter)
#
# Neither half is reachable by changing a path constant. The first requires the rule to ignore this
# file; the second requires the score to know the difference.
standardVersion: "1.0.0"
project: "wrong-root-broken"

mathematics:
  regimes:
    - informal
  claimsLedger: "artifacts/claims-ledger.md"

cases.name: 0288fce:test/fixtures/wrong-root-clean/project-policy.yml
cases.input:
# The third adopter state: a provenance record of its own that is CORRECT.
#
# The discriminating fixture for step 6's architectural question. `wrong-root-broken` shows that an
# adopter's drifted record does not make the framework's integrity rule fail; this one shows the
# other half, which is the half that would flatter rather than punish: an adopter's intact record
# does not make it pass either.
#
# Together the three states — record absent, record drifted, record intact — settle the question a
# single fixture cannot:
#
#   framework-ownership reading   the result is IDENTICAL across all three. The adopter's file is
#                                 not the subject, and nothing the adopter does to it registers.
#   adopter-root reading          the result VARIES with all three, and enters the adopter's score.
#
# Invariance across the three is a property no path constant can fake, and it is what the test
# asserts. See design/v1.2-evidence-provenance.md §13.
standardVersion: "1.0.0"
project: "wrong-root-clean"

mathematics:
  regimes:
    - informal
  claimsLedger: "artifacts/claims-ledger.md"
